A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Evolutionary Prediction Games by the same authors. Their main texts, equations, figures, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across reordered experiments and renumbered figures.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic simulations, MNIST and CIFAR-10 classifier experiments, and simulated population dynamics, including stabilization results.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds ACSIncome experiments and analyses of sampling noise, convergence, stabilization sensitivity, and different learning algorithms.

M1.justification: The prediction-game framework, learning constructions, and stabilization rule A'(p) = Aopt(2p* - p) are retained. Gaussian-process modeling and additional classifiers are introduced for empirical analysis; they do not revise the proposed learning or stabilization procedure.

E1.justification: Section 6.3 adds ACSIncome income classification using 2018 California, New York, and Texas census populations. This substantially extends the empirical coverage from synthetic examples and two-group image tasks to tabular socioeconomic data and three real-data groups. MNIST and CIFAR-10 remain.

E2.justification: Appendix F.4 introduces an explicit comparison of linear SVM, logistic regression, and XGBoost on ACSIncome, with their induced dynamics displayed in Figure 14. This adds a focused comparison of underlying learners; the original comparison between ordinary and stabilized learning remains.

E3.justification: Existing MNIST and CIFAR-10 protocols are retained. New protocols include ACSIncome training samples of 1,000 with 5,000 held-out examples per state, Gaussian-process stochastic fitness with covariance multipliers 0, 1, and 5, convergence measured at a 1% minority threshold, and sweeps over initial conditions and estimated stabilization targets.

E4.justification: New Appendix F tests whether sampling noise changes eventual dominance, how initial composition affects convergence time, how equilibrium-estimation errors affect stabilization, and how learner choice changes three-group dynamics. These substantially extend the existing regularization and k-NN analyses, which are retained.

E5.justification: The existing 20 CIFAR-10 repetitions, 50 MNIST repetitions, and 99% confidence level remain. v3 adds ten-repetition ACSIncome averaging and reports observation and Gaussian-process standard deviations in Figure 12. Appendix E no longer specifies that its mean confidence intervals are normal-based; no increase in existing experiment run counts is established.

E6.justification: Original headline accuracies remain unchanged: CIFAR-10 reports 92.6 ± 0.1% at dominance and 93.5 ± 0.1% at coexistence; MNIST reports 80.4 ± 0.2%. New ACSIncome results show disparity falling from approximately 2 to 0.2 percentage points after NY's share falls below 1%. Appendix F adds noise-dependent outcomes, convergence and stabilization-sensitivity curves, and different endpoints for SVM, logistic regression, and XGBoost.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix D.2 explicitly formulate Nash stationarity and imitative dynamics as alternatives, whereas v2 handled imitative dynamics through an exception. Appendix D.3.2 additionally states that the fairness correspondence extends to restricted equilibria. The main theorems, constructions, and substantive proofs otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and concluding discussion retain the same central claims: oracle retraining promotes competitive exclusion, practical learning constraints can enable coexistence, and dynamics-aware stabilization can sustain it. The fairness concern already appears in v2; its new experiment supplies evidence rather than a new core claim.

C2.justification: Appendix A substantially expands discussion of observed diversity and practical retention or recruitment interventions. Appendix F adds interpretations concerning weak selection near balanced populations, stabilization errors affecting composition while preserving welfare in the examined setting, and learner-dependent applicability of two-phase fairness dynamics. These extend the original interpretation and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v3 documents ACSIncome classifier implementations and default regularization, plus Gaussian-process settings including RBF length scale 0.1 and alpha 4. Reported synthetic-pipeline runtime changes from roughly 20 to 30 minutes. Existing architecture details, hardware, and code-access information remain.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted fairness, application, dataset, and software citations, including Barocas et al., Dwork et al., and Chaney et al., while removing several background references. Sections 1.1 and B refine the fairness positioning, but the central relationships to performative prediction and Hashimoto et al. remain. Publication updates to retained references are bibliographic changes.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and most prose remain. v3 reverses the MNIST/CIFAR-10 subsection order, reorganizes the fairness discussion in Section 3, expands Appendix A with descriptive subheadings, and adds Sections 6.3 and F. Local wording and cross-references are revised, without extensive rewriting of the existing paper.

P2.justification: New multipanel Figures 5 and 12–14 substantially expand the visual evidence with population trajectories, uncertainty displays, convergence and sensitivity curves, and comparative phase portraits. Figure 13 also redisplays the CIFAR-10 game after smoothing. Existing Figure 4 moves, and v2 Figures 5–10 are retained as v3 Figures 6–11.

improvement.justification: The ACSIncome case study gives empirical support to the previously conceptual fairness concern, while Appendix F tests previously unexamined noise and stabilization sensitivities. Clearer assumptions and applicability discussion also help interpretation. These are useful but bounded gains: population responses remain simulated, and the central theoretical contribution is retained. Minor drafting and cross-reference slips limit the improvement in presentation.
